concepts.name: GST on a price
concepts.description: GST is a percentage of the price before tax. Adding it: base × (1 + r/100). Taking it out of a tax-inclusive price: base = inclusive × 100/(100 + r), and the GST inside is r/(100 + r) of the bill.

concepts.name: CGST, SGST and IGST
concepts.description: A sale within one state carries CGST and SGST, each half the GST rate. A sale between states carries IGST at the full rate. The total tax is the same either way.

concepts.name: GST through a supply chain
concepts.description: Each trader charges GST on its sale and claims back the GST it paid on its purchase (input tax credit), so it pays GST only on the value it adds. Together the chain pays exactly GST on the final price.

concepts.name: Discount, sales tax and VAT
concepts.description: GST, sales tax or VAT is charged on the price after any discount. A discount and a tax are successive percentage changes, so their order does not change the final price: marked × (1 − d/100) × (1 + t/100).

concepts.name: Income tax with slabs
concepts.description: Taxable income = gross income − deductions. Each slab rate applies only to the part of the income inside that slab; a rebate can cancel the tax below a limit, and cess is a percentage of the tax.

concepts.name: Commission and brokerage
concepts.description: Commission is a percentage of sales; earnings may add a fixed salary. Tiered commission works like slabs: each rate on its own band of sales. Brokerage is a broker’s commission on a deal.

concepts.name: Property tax and customs duty
concepts.description: Property tax is a rate on a property’s annual value, sometimes less a rebate for paying early. On imports, duty is charged on the assessable value and IGST on the value plus the duty.

formulas.title: Adding GST
formulas.prompt: An item costs P before GST at r%. What is the GST, and what does the buyer pay?
formulas.formula:
GST = P × r/100
Price paid = P × (1 + r/100)
formulas.explanation: GST is always worked out on the price before tax.
formulas.commonMistake: Giving the GST alone as the price, or dividing by 1.12 instead of multiplying.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A ₹6,500 phone attracts 18% GST. What does the buyer pay?

formulas.title: Taking GST out of an inclusive price
formulas.prompt: A bill of ₹B includes GST at r%. What was the price before GST, and how much is GST?
formulas.formula:
Price before GST = B × 100/(100 + r)
GST = B × r/(100 + r)
formulas.explanation: The bill is (100 + r)% of the price before tax, so divide by (100 + r) and multiply by 100.
formulas.commonMistake: Taking r% of the inclusive price (₹3,186 here), which taxes the tax.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A bill of ₹1,050 includes 5% GST. What was the price before GST?

formulas.title: CGST, SGST and IGST
formulas.prompt: How is GST at r% shown on a bill within a state, and on one between states?
formulas.formula:
Within a state: CGST = SGST = r/2 % each
Between states: IGST = r %
formulas.explanation: The total tax is the same; only how it is labelled (and which government receives it) changes.
formulas.example: ₹3,500 at 18% within a state: CGST ₹315 + SGST ₹315. Between states: IGST ₹630.
formulas.commonMistake: Charging CGST and SGST each at the full rate.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A ₹2,000 sale from Kolkata to Patna at 12%: what tax goes on the bill?

formulas.title: Input tax credit
formulas.prompt: A trader buys for C and sells for S, both plus GST at r%. How much GST does it pay the government?
formulas.formula:
Net GST = r% of S − r% of C = r% of (S − C)
Whole chain: total GST = r% of the final price
formulas.explanation: The GST paid on the purchase is credited against the GST collected on the sale, so only the value added is taxed.
formulas.commonMistake: Paying GST on the full sale and forgetting the credit.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A retailer buys for ₹40,000 and sells for ₹46,000 at 12%. What GST does it pay?

formulas.title: Discount, then tax
formulas.prompt: Marked price M, discount d%, then tax t% on the discounted price. What is paid?
formulas.explanation: Tax is charged on what is actually charged for the goods: the price after discount. Multiplication does not care about order.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A ₹8,000 jacket at 15% off with 18% GST: what is paid?

formulas.title: Tax on slabs
formulas.prompt: How is income tax worked out from a slab table?
formulas.formula:
Taxable income = gross − deductions
Tax = Σ (slab rate × part of taxable income in that slab)
formulas.explanation: Each rate applies only to the slice of income inside its slab, so crossing into a higher slab never taxes the lower slices more.
formulas.example: Slabs nil to ₹3 lakh, 5% to ₹6 lakh, 10% to ₹9 lakh: on ₹8.4 lakh, 5% of 3 lakh + 10% of 2.4 lakh = ₹39,000.
formulas.commonMistake: Charging the top rate on the whole income.
formulas.applicationPrompt: With the same slabs, what is the tax on ₹5,00,000?

formulas.title: Rebate and cess
formulas.prompt: After slab tax, how are a rebate and a cess applied?
formulas.formula:
Tax after rebate = slab tax − rebate (only if taxable income is within the limit)
Total = tax after rebate × (1 + cess/100)
formulas.explanation: A rebate is subtracted from the tax; cess is a percentage of the tax that is left, not of the income.
formulas.commonMistake: Testing the rebate limit against gross salary instead of taxable income.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Slab tax is ₹15,000 on a taxable income within the rebate limit, rebate up to ₹20,000. What is due?

formulas.title: Commission
formulas.prompt: How are flat, salary-plus and tiered commission worked out?
formulas.formula:
Commission = rate × sales
Earnings = fixed pay + rate × sales
Tiered: each rate on its own band of sales
formulas.explanation: A tiered scheme is a slab table for sales. To find the sales for a target, take off the fixed pay first, then divide by the rate.
formulas.example: 4% on the first ₹2 lakh and 6% above: on ₹3.5 lakh, ₹8,000 + ₹9,000 = ₹17,000.
formulas.commonMistake: Paying the top rate on all sales, or forgetting the fixed pay when working backwards.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Fixed ₹12,000 plus 5% on sales: what sales give ₹30,000 a month?

formulas.title: Property tax and customs duty
formulas.prompt: How are property tax and customs duty on an import worked out?
formulas.formula:
Property tax = rate × annual value (less any rebate on the tax)
Customs: duty = rate × value; IGST = rate × (value + duty)
formulas.explanation: Rates here are examples stated in a question; the rule to remember is the base each rate is charged on.
formulas.commonMistake: Charging IGST on the value alone, before the duty is added.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A house with annual value ₹1,80,000 is taxed at 9%. What is the tax?

formulas.title: GST hidden in a bill
formulas.prompt: What fraction of a GST-inclusive bill is tax, at 5%, 12% and 18%?
formulas.explanation: One division instead of two steps: the share of tax in the bill depends only on the rate.
formulas.commonMistake: Using r/100 of the bill (18% of ₹17,700 = ₹3,186).
formulas.applicationPrompt: How much GST is inside a ₹2,100 bill at 5%?

formulas.title: The chain pays GST on the final price
formulas.prompt: With input credit at every stage, how much GST does the government get from a whole supply chain?
formulas.formula:
Total GST = r% × final selling price
(the earlier prices cancel out)
formulas.explanation: Each trader pays on its value added, and the values added sum to the final price.
formulas.example: Sold on at ₹12,000 then ₹15,000 at 18%: the government gets 18% of ₹15,000 = ₹2,700.
formulas.commonMistake: Adding the GST on every sale (₹2,160 + ₹2,700 = ₹4,860), which ignores the credit.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Prices ₹40,000, ₹52,000, ₹65,000 at 5%: what does the government receive in all?

formulas.title: Discount and tax as one change
formulas.prompt: A d% discount and a t% tax together change the marked price by what percentage?
formulas.explanation: The successive-change rule. The −td/100 is the tax saved on the discount.
formulas.applicationPrompt: What single change equals 20% off followed by 18% GST?

levels.title: Taxes on a Price, and Who Pays Them
levels.description: Add GST and take it out of a bill, split it into CGST and SGST or IGST, follow it through a supply chain, then meet slabs, commission and duties.

blocks.title: GST is a percentage of the price before tax
blocks.body:
If an item costs ₹2,400 before GST and the rate is 12%, the GST is 12% of ₹2,400 = ₹288 and the buyer pays ₹2,688, that is ₹2,400 × 1.12.

Going the other way, a bill that already includes GST is (100 + r)% of the base: divide by 1 + r/100 to find the price before tax. Never take r% of the bill: that taxes the tax.

blocks.title: Within a state, or between states
blocks.body: A sale inside one state carries central GST (CGST) and state GST (SGST), each at half the rate: 18% becomes 9% + 9%. A sale from one state to another carries integrated GST (IGST) at the full rate. The buyer pays the same total either way; only the labels change.

blocks.title: Tax only on the value added
blocks.body:
Goods often pass through several hands. Each trader charges GST on its sale, but claims back the GST it paid when buying: the input tax credit. So each pays GST only on the value it adds, and the whole chain together pays exactly GST on the final price.

Move the prices in the simulation and watch the total stay at r% of the retailer’s price.

blocks.title: Discount and tax together
blocks.caption: GST, sales tax or VAT is charged on the discounted price. The two changes multiply, so their order does not matter: ₹30,000 with 10% off and 12% GST is ₹30,240 either way.

blocks.title: Slabs, tiers and duties
blocks.body:
Income tax on slabs taxes each slice of income at its own rate: crossing into a higher slab does not raise the tax on the lower slices. Tiered commission works the same way on sales. Customs duty is charged on the value of an import, and IGST on the value plus the duty.

Questions always give the slabs and rates to use. The tables in this topic are examples, not the current law.

The usual traps: tax on the wrong base (the bill instead of the price before tax, the marked price instead of the discounted one), the input credit forgotten, and the top slab rate charged on the whole income.

levels.title: GST, Brokerage and Slabs: First Steps
levels.description: One-step GST, bills within and between states, brokerage and a first slab.

levels.title: Inclusive Prices, Input Credit and Discounts
levels.description: Take GST out of a bill, follow tax along a supply chain, and combine a discount with GST.

levels.title: Income Tax, Commission and Property Tax

levels.title: Mixed Taxes and Commission Practice

questions.question: A pressure cooker in a Madurai shop is priced at ₹2,400 before GST. GST on it is 12%. How much does the buyer pay?
questions.explanation: GST = 12% of ₹2,400 = ₹288. The buyer pays the price plus the tax: ₹2,400 + ₹288 = ₹2,688 (the same as ₹2,400 × 1.12).
questions.method: Price with GST = base × (1 + r/100).

hints.text: GST is charged on the price before tax, ₹2,400.
12% of ₹2,400 is ₹288; add it to the price.

commonMistakes: Giving the GST alone (₹288) as the answer.
Dividing by 1.12 (₹2,142.86), which takes GST out instead of adding it.

questions.question: A restaurant bill in Chennai shows ₹1,050, including GST at 5%. What was the price of the meal before GST (in ₹)?
questions.explanation: The bill is 105% of the price before GST. ₹1,050 × 100/105 = ₹1,000. Check: 5% of ₹1,000 is ₹50, and ₹1,000 + ₹50 = ₹1,050.
questions.method: Base = inclusive × 100/(100 + r).

hints.text: ₹1,050 already includes the 5%. What percentage of the base is it?
Divide ₹1,050 by 1.05.

questions.question: A shop in Pune sells a ceiling fan to a customer in Pune for ₹3,500 plus GST at 18%. How is the tax shown on the bill?
questions.explanation: GST = 18% of ₹3,500 = ₹630. Seller and buyer are both in Maharashtra, so it is a sale within a state: the 18% is split into 9% CGST and 9% SGST, ₹315 each.
solutionSteps: Same state: CGST and SGST, half each.
questions.method: Within a state, CGST = SGST = half the GST.

hints.text: Are the shop and the customer in the same state?
Within a state, the 18% is shared equally between the Centre and the state.

commonMistakes: Using IGST for a sale inside one state.
Charging CGST and SGST each at the full 18%.

questions.question: A firm in Ahmedabad (Gujarat) sells goods worth ₹50,000 to a firm in Jaipur (Rajasthan) at 12% GST. The bill should show CGST of 6% and SGST of 6%.
questions.explanation: The goods move from Gujarat to Rajasthan, so this is a sale between states. It carries IGST at the full 12% (₹6,000), not CGST and SGST.
solutionSteps: Seller in Gujarat, buyer in Rajasthan: two different states.
A sale between states carries IGST.
IGST = 12% of ₹50,000 = ₹6,000, so the statement is false.
questions.method: Same state: CGST + SGST. Different states: IGST.

hints.text: Check the states of the seller and the buyer.
Which kind of GST applies when goods cross a state border?

commonMistakes: Splitting the rate into CGST and SGST whatever the states.

questions.question: A property broker in Kochi charges the seller 2% brokerage. He arranges the sale of a flat for ₹45,00,000. How much brokerage does he get from the seller?
questions.method: Brokerage = rate × value of the deal.

hints.text: The broker charges 2% of the price.

commonMistakes: Misplacing the decimal point: ₹9,000 (0.2%) or ₹9,00,000 (20%).
Charging 2% to both buyer and seller when only the seller pays.

questions.question: An item has marked price P. The shop gives a 10% discount and then charges 18% GST on the discounted price. Which expression gives the amount paid?
questions.explanation: A 10% discount leaves 0.90 of P; 18% GST on that multiplies by 1.18. So the amount paid is P × 0.90 × 1.18 = 1.062P. Netting the rates (1.08P) forgets that GST is charged on the smaller, discounted price.
questions.method: Successive percentage changes multiply.

hints.text: Write each change as a multiplier.
A 10% discount is × 0.90; 18% GST is × 1.18.

commonMistakes: Adding the rates: 1 + 0.18 − 0.10 = 1.08.
Writing the GST as ₹18 instead of 18%.

questions.question: Use these example slabs (an illustration for this question, not the current law). Ravi’s taxable income for the year is ₹5,00,000. How much income tax does he pay?

table.caption: Example income tax slabs, for this question only (not the current law)

questions.explanation: The first ₹3,00,000 is tax-free. The remaining ₹2,00,000 lies in the 5% slab: 5% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹10,000.
questions.method: Tax only the part of income inside each slab.

hints.text: How much of ₹5,00,000 is above the tax-free limit?
That part is taxed at 5%.

commonMistakes: Charging 5% on the whole ₹5,00,000 (₹25,000).
Thinking an income in the 5% slab pays nothing.

questions.question: A mobile phone costs ₹17,700, including GST at 18%. How much of that is GST (in ₹)?
questions.explanation: The price is 118% of the price before GST, so GST is 18/118 of it: ₹17,700 × 18/118 = ₹2,700. Check: the base is ₹15,000 and 18% of ₹15,000 is ₹2,700.
questions.method: GST in an inclusive price = price × r/(100 + r).

hints.text: ₹17,700 is not the base: it already includes the 18%.
GST is 18/118 (= 9/59) of the inclusive price.

commonMistakes: Taking 18% of ₹17,700 (₹3,186), which taxes the tax.

questions.question: In Coimbatore, a manufacturer sells shirts to a wholesaler for ₹40,000; the wholesaler sells them to a retailer for ₹52,000; the retailer sells them to customers for ₹65,000. GST is 5% at every stage and all sales are within Tamil Nadu. How much GST does the retailer pay to the government?
questions.explanation: The retailer collects 5% of ₹65,000 = ₹3,250 from customers, but has already paid 5% of ₹52,000 = ₹2,600 to the wholesaler. It claims that as input tax credit and pays ₹3,250 − ₹2,600 = ₹650: 5% of the value it added, ₹13,000.
questions.method: Net GST = r% of (selling price − buying price).

hints.text: What GST did the retailer already pay when it bought the shirts?
It pays only on the value it adds: ₹65,000 − ₹52,000.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the input credit (₹3,250).
Taking credit from the manufacturer’s price instead of the wholesaler’s (₹1,250), or working out the wholesaler’s tax (₹600) instead.

questions.question: A furniture maker in Jodhpur sells a dining table to a dealer for ₹12,000 plus 18% GST. The dealer sells it to a customer for ₹15,000 plus 18% GST. Both claim input tax credit where they can. How much GST, in all, reaches the government (in ₹)?
questions.explanation: The maker pays 18% of ₹12,000 = ₹2,160. The dealer collects 18% of ₹15,000 = ₹2,700 but takes credit for the ₹2,160 it paid, so it pays ₹540. Total = ₹2,160 + ₹540 = ₹2,700, which is simply 18% of the final price ₹15,000.
questions.method: With input credit, the whole chain pays r% of the final price.

hints.text: Does the dealer pay the full ₹2,700, or does it get something back?
Each stage pays only on its value added; the values added sum to ₹15,000.

commonMistakes: Adding the GST on both sales: ₹2,160 + ₹2,700 = ₹4,860.

questions.question: A refrigerator has a marked price of ₹30,000. The shop gives a 10% discount and then charges 12% GST on the discounted price. What does the customer pay?

hints.text: GST is charged after the discount.

commonMistakes: Netting the rates, 12% − 10% = 2% (₹30,600).
Ignoring the discount (₹33,600) or the GST (₹27,000).

questions.question: For a ₹8,000 jacket, a 15% discount followed by 18% GST on the discounted price gives the same final price as adding 18% GST first and then taking 15% off the tax-inclusive price.
questions.explanation: Both orders multiply ₹8,000 by the same two factors: 8,000 × 0.85 × 1.18 = ₹8,024 and 8,000 × 1.18 × 0.85 = ₹8,024. Successive percentage changes can be applied in either order.
questions.method: Multiplication is commutative.

hints.text: Write each change as a multiplier.

commonMistakes: Thinking the buyer saves by taking the discount first.

questions.question: A television is advertised in Lucknow at ₹35,400, including 18% GST. In a sale, the shop takes 10% off the price before GST and then adds the GST. How much less (in ₹) does a buyer pay in the sale?
questions.explanation: Price before GST = ₹35,400 × 100/118 = ₹30,000. After 10% off: ₹27,000. With 18% GST: ₹31,860. Saving = ₹35,400 − ₹31,860 = ₹3,540, which is exactly 10% of the original bill, since the GST is charged on a price 10% lower.
questions.method: Take the GST out, apply the discount, put the GST back; or note that 10% off the base is 10% off the bill.

hints.text: First find the price before GST.
A 10% cut in the base cuts the GST by 10% too.

commonMistakes: Answering ₹3,000, the cut in the base alone, forgetting the GST saved on it.

questions.question: Use these example slabs (an illustration for this question, not the current law). Meena’s taxable income is ₹8,40,000. How much income tax is due (in ₹)?

table.caption: Example income tax slabs, for this question only (not the current law)

questions.explanation: The first ₹3,00,000 is tax-free. The next ₹3,00,000 (up to ₹6,00,000) is taxed at 5%: ₹15,000. The remaining ₹2,40,000 is in the 10% slab: ₹24,000. Total = ₹39,000.
questions.method: Tax each slice of income at its own rate.

hints.text: Split ₹8,40,000 into the slabs: 3 lakh + 3 lakh + 2.4 lakh.
Only the last ₹2,40,000 is taxed at 10%.

commonMistakes: Charging 10% on the whole ₹8,40,000 (₹84,000).

questions.question: Use these example slabs (an illustration for this question, not the current law). Arjun earns ₹9,50,000 a year and claims deductions of ₹1,50,000. How much income tax does he pay?

table.caption: Example income tax slabs, for this question only (not the current law)

questions.method: Deduct first, then apply the slabs.

hints.text: Slabs apply to taxable income, not gross income.
Taxable income is ₹8,00,000.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the deduction (₹52,500).
Charging 10% on all ₹8,00,000 (₹80,000), or counting only the top slice (₹20,000).

questions.question: A salesperson at a Delhi electronics store gets 4% commission on the first ₹2,00,000 of monthly sales and 6% on sales above ₹2,00,000. In March she sells goods worth ₹3,50,000. What is her commission (in ₹)?
questions.explanation: 4% of the first ₹2,00,000 = ₹8,000. The other ₹1,50,000 earns 6%: ₹9,000. Commission = ₹17,000.
questions.method: Tiered commission: each rate on its own band.

hints.text: Split the sales at ₹2,00,000.
Only the ₹1,50,000 above the limit earns 6%.

commonMistakes: Paying 6% on all sales (₹21,000).

questions.question: Imran, a medical representative in Hyderabad, gets a fixed ₹12,000 a month plus 5% commission on his sales. How much must he sell in a month to earn ₹30,000 in all?
questions.explanation: The commission has to make up ₹30,000 − ₹12,000 = ₹18,000. That is 5% of sales, so sales = ₹18,000 × 100/5 = ₹3,60,000.
questions.method: Sales = (target − fixed pay) ÷ rate.

hints.text: How much of the ₹30,000 must come from commission?
₹18,000 is 5% of the sales.

commonMistakes: Dividing the whole ₹30,000 by 5% (₹6,00,000).
Adding the salary instead of subtracting it (₹8,40,000).

questions.question: A municipality charges property tax at 9% of a house’s annual value (an example rate), and gives a 5% rebate on the tax to owners who pay before 30 April. A house in Madurai has an annual value of ₹1,80,000. How much (in ₹) does an owner who pays early pay?
questions.explanation: Tax = 9% of ₹1,80,000 = ₹16,200. The rebate is 5% of the tax, ₹810, so the owner pays ₹16,200 − ₹810 = ₹15,390.
questions.method: Tax on the annual value, then the rebate on the tax.

hints.text: Find 9% of ₹1,80,000 first.
The 5% rebate is taken off the tax, not off the annual value.

commonMistakes: Subtracting 5 from the rate (4% of ₹1,80,000 = ₹7,200).

questions.question: A manufacturer in Surat (Gujarat) sells goods to a dealer in Nagpur (Maharashtra) for ₹50,000 plus 12% GST. The dealer sells them to a shop in Nagpur for ₹62,000 plus 12% GST. After using its input tax credit, how much GST does the dealer pay the government in all?
questions.explanation: The first sale crosses states, so the dealer paid IGST of 12% of ₹50,000 = ₹6,000. Its own sale is within Maharashtra, so it charges CGST + SGST of 12% of ₹62,000 = ₹7,440 in all. The IGST it paid is credited against this tax, leaving ₹7,440 − ₹6,000 = ₹1,440 to pay: 12% of the ₹12,000 it added.
questions.method: Credit for tax paid on purchase, whatever its label; pay on the value added.

hints.text: What tax did the dealer pay when it bought the goods from Gujarat?
That IGST is credited against the CGST and SGST it collects.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the credit because the labels differ (₹7,440).
Halving the answer as if only CGST were asked (₹720).

questions.question: Deepa paid ₹23,600 for a sofa in Bengaluru, after a 20% discount on the marked price and then 18% GST on the discounted price. What was the marked price (in ₹)?
questions.explanation: Undo the steps in reverse order. Before GST: ₹23,600 × 100/118 = ₹20,000. That was 80% of the marked price: ₹20,000 × 100/80 = ₹25,000. Check: 25,000 × 0.8 × 1.18 = ₹23,600.

hints.text: First take the 18% GST out by dividing by 1.18.
₹20,000 is 80% of the marked price.

commonMistakes: Adding 20% back to ₹20,000 (₹24,000) instead of dividing by 0.8.

questions.question: Use these example slabs (an illustration for this question, not the current law). Also take these example rules: a standard deduction of ₹75,000; a rebate that cancels the tax, up to ₹25,000, when taxable income is at most ₹7,00,000; and a cess of 4% on the tax left. Priya’s gross salary is ₹8,50,000. What is her total tax?

table.caption: Example income tax slabs, for this question only (not the current law)

questions.method: Deduct, tax by slabs, check the rebate, add cess.

hints.text: Find taxable income first.
Is ₹7,75,000 within the rebate limit?
Cess is 4% of the tax, not of the income.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the cess (₹32,500) or the standard deduction (₹41,600).
Applying the rebate although income is above the limit (₹0).

questions.question: A broker in Jaipur arranges the sale of a plot for ₹60,00,000. He charges the seller 1.5% and the buyer 1% as brokerage, and pays 25% of his total brokerage to a sub-agent who found the buyer. How much brokerage (in ₹) does he keep?
questions.explanation: From the seller: 1.5% of ₹60,00,000 = ₹90,000. From the buyer: 1% = ₹60,000. Total brokerage = ₹1,50,000. The sub-agent gets 25% = ₹37,500, so the broker keeps ₹1,12,500 (75% of ₹1,50,000).
questions.method: Add both sides’ brokerage, then take the share given away.

hints.text: Brokerage comes from both the seller and the buyer.

questions.question: An importer in Chennai brings in machinery with an assessable value of ₹4,00,000. Take (as an example) a basic customs duty of 10% on the assessable value, and then IGST of 18% on the value plus the duty. How much tax is paid in all?
questions.method: Duty on the value; IGST on value + duty.

hints.text: Work out the duty first.
IGST is charged on the value with the duty added.

commonMistakes: Charging IGST on ₹4,00,000 alone (₹1,12,000).
Giving the IGST or the duty alone.

questions.question: A Kolkata firm makes four sales of ₹2,000 each. Match each sale to the tax on its bill.

pairs.left: To a Kolkata customer, at 12% GST
To a Patna firm, at 12% GST
To a Kolkata customer, at 18% GST
To a Patna firm, at 18% GST

questions.explanation: Kolkata to Kolkata is within West Bengal: half the rate each as CGST and SGST. Kolkata to Patna crosses into Bihar: the full rate as IGST. 12% of ₹2,000 = ₹240 and 18% of ₹2,000 = ₹360.
solutionSteps: Within West Bengal: split in half (₹120 + ₹120, ₹180 + ₹180).
To Bihar: IGST at the full amount (₹240, ₹360).
questions.method: Same state: halves; different states: whole as IGST.

hints.text: Which sales cross a state border?
Each CGST or SGST line is half the total GST.

commonMistakes: Showing the full GST as CGST and again as SGST.

questions.question: Goods pass from a manufacturer to a wholesaler to a retailer, and the retailer sells them for ₹10,000 plus 18% GST. Every trader claims input tax credit. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The government collects ₹1,800 in all, whatever the earlier prices were.
Each trader pays 18% of the value it adds.
The retailer pays ₹1,800 to the government.
Without input credit, the total tax collected would be more than ₹1,800.
If the wholesaler raises its price, the total tax collected rises.

questions.explanation: Each trader pays 18% of its value added, and the values added sum to the final ₹10,000, so the total is ₹1,800 (A and B true). The retailer pays only on its own value added, less than ₹10,000 (C false). Without credit, every earlier sale would be taxed again: more than ₹1,800 (D true). A higher wholesale price shifts tax from the retailer to the wholesaler but leaves the total at 18% of ₹10,000 (E false).
solutionSteps: Retailer’s share = 18% of (10,000 − its buying price) < ₹1,800.
Raising a middle price moves tax between traders; the total is unchanged.
questions.method: Total GST depends only on the final price.

hints.text: What does each trader pay tax on?
Add up the values added along the chain.

commonMistakes: Thinking the retailer pays all the tax on the final price.
Thinking middle prices change the total.
